messages.content: Each section must begin with a thesis statement in italics, use HTML to indicate the italics. Write a story about a hedgehog with glasses, the only real creature in an abstract world, resembling abstract art

message.content: The world was not a place but a painting, and Quill was the only living brushstroke that could not be admired from a distance. There were no trees. There were no roads. There were no rivers or mountains or even a horizon, because the horizon had been painted over in a thick, confident smear of cadmium yellow that extended in every direction until it became indistinguishable from the sky. Quill, a hedgehog no larger than a man's fist, perched atop a flat expanse of matte black paint and blinked behind his round brass-rimmed glasses. He adjusted them with one tiny claw, pushing them up the bridge of his nose, and looked out at the landscape. It was a Rothko field—vast, layered, humming with a deep violet that shifted to burnt sienna near the edges. The color breathed. Not like wind moving through grass, but like color *breathing*, as if the pigment itself had a slow pulmonary rhythm. Quill had lived in this world for what he estimated to be a long time, though time here was a thick impasto ridge he could feel under his belly, uneven and slow. Reality was a foreign language in a country of pure form, and Quill spoke it badly, stubbornly, with the grammar of a small spine-tipped body. He walked. His feet, four of them, bare-pink and furred, pressed into the flat surface of the black field, and where they touched, the paint did not smear. It *held*. This was the strange miracle of him: the abstract world, for all its confident geometry and gestural splatter, could not unmake him. When he stepped onto a canvas of Pollock-esque drips—silver and gold and sharp white lines whipping across a ground of raw umber—his paws found purchase on the ridged paint. The splatters did not flow around him. They stopped, as if the chaos had a border, a personal space he had willed into existence simply by being *there*, a small warm *there* with a heartbeat. He wore his glasses because the world was so full of visual noise. Without them, the overlapping color fields blurred into a single, unbearable hum. With them, the lenses caught the light in small, precise circles, and he could parse the shapes. A geometric red square, three times the length of his body, sat to the east. It did not move. It had not moved in what he estimated to be years. To the north, a long gestural sweep of cobalt stretched like a river, but it was only paint, dry and still, catching no wind. In a world of infinite color and shape, the one thing that could not be described was the sound of a tiny foot hitting a flat plane of cerulean blue. It was the sound that kept him sane. *Tap. Tap. Tap.* The small, dry, almost imperceptible percussion of a living foot on a dead surface. No one heard it—there was no one. The world had no other ears, no other eyes, no other small warm body to generate its own private percussion. Quill crossed the cobalt sweep at an angle, his spines catching the light in a scatter of tiny points, and felt the dry ridge of the brushstroke under his belly. He paused. He tilted his head, pushing his glasses up again, and stared at the red square. It was so still. So *certain*. It did not wonder. It did not adjust its glasses. It simply *was*, a perfect rectangle of vermillion that had been decided upon by an invisible hand and then left alone. Quill felt the small, aching pull of loneliness he always felt in this place, but he did not name it. Naming things here was dangerous; words were shapes, and shapes were paint, and if he said *lonely* out loud, the word might seep into the nearest field and become a shapeless smear of grey he would have to walk around for a week. So he simply turned, and he walked, and the *tap tap tap* continued, the only rhythm in a world of frozen color. Quill did not need to understand the world to be real in it, and that was enough. He reached the edge of the black field where it met a raw, unpainted stretch of gesso—pale, chalky, the color of nothing yet. He sat down. He pulled a small, folded piece of fabric from inside his belly fur (a habit he had developed long ago; the fabric was a scrap of canvas, off-white, the only material in the world that had once been a *thing* before it became a *surface*). He unfolded it, folded it again, unfolded it. His glasses caught the flat light and threw two small, round halos onto the gesso. The halos were the only things in the entire world that moved, that *lived*, that belonged to a small creature who breathed and bled and felt the cold of the pigment against his paws at night. He blinked. The halos blinked with him. Somewhere far to the west, a field of ultramarine shifted one degree toward indigo, and the cadmium yellow horizon pulsed, slow as a sleeping heart. The red square sat. The cobalt sweep stretched. The drips dried. And Quill, small and spined and glasses-bright, sat at the edge of the unpainted, and tapped his foot once, twice, three times, against the flat, and the sound was small, and the sound was real, and the sound was the only sound there would ever be, and that was enough.
